Ensemble Methodology for Reference-Free Confidence Estimation in LLM-based Code Summarization
Marco Colombomcolom4@illinois.eduUniversity of Illinois Urbana-ChampaignSumit Tokkarstokkar@illinois.eduUniversity of Illinois Urbana-ChampaignBalaji A JBalaji_Jayaram@infosys.comInfosysSowmyakumari Selvarajsowmyakumari.s@infosys.comInfosysAnimesh Kumaranimesh.kumar14@infosys.comInfosysRavishankar ShettyRavishankarS@infosys.comInfosysAravinda Prasad Sistlasistla@uic.eduUniversity of Illinois ChicagoRigel Gjomemorgjome1@uic.eduUniversity of Illinois ChicagoAbstract.
This paper describes an approach and use case to estimate the correctness of LLM-generated COBOL summaries without access to human-authored references. The core intuition is that inter-model agreement on semantics is informative about truth, and that an LLM-as-judge can provide higher-fidelity pairwise assessments than traditional string- or embedding-based metrics (Wu et al., 2024; Robinson and Kummerfeld, 2025). We operationalise this intuition with (i) controlled summary generation from diverse models; (ii) a LLM evaluator that compares pairs of summaries and emits structured judgments; and (iii) a calibrated aggregation rule that combines supportive evidence while penalising only corroborated contradictions.
1.Introduction
COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) remains deeply entrenched in enterprise computing, with billions of lines of code in production across financial services, insurance, government, and healthcare sectors (Britton, 2024). These legacy systems, developed over several decades, manage mission-critical operations including transaction processing platforms (IBM TPF), core banking systems, claims processing, and regulatory compliance frameworks. The technical complexity of these codebases stems from decades of incremental modifications, vendor-specific extensions, and business logic that evolved without adequate documentation, creating significant knowledge management challenges for organizations maintaining these systems.The imperative for COBOL modernization stems from multiple converging factors. First, the steep decline in COBOL-proficient developers—with a significant portion of existing practitioners approaching retirement age and limited new talent entering the field—creates a critical sustainability risk. Second, integration challenges between legacy COBOL platforms and modern cloud-native architectures, microservices, and API ecosystems impede digital transformation initiatives. Third, maintaining aging mainframe infrastructure incurs substantial costs. These factors have given rise to multiple initiatives aimed to transform COBOL codebases into modern languages and platforms (Gandhi et al., 2024; Chakravarthy et al., 2026). Some of these initiatives include direct translation of COBOL codebases into a modern language (Chakaravarthy et al., 2026; Froimovich et al., 2025; Challa et al., 2025) while others are focused on extracting specifications and the business logic, which can then be used to recreate that business logic in a modern language and architecture (Bhattacharyya et al., 2025; Kalohia, 2026).In this paper, we are focused on the latter approach, business logic extraction from COBOL codebases. The main challenge in this approach is that the vast majority of legacy COBOL programs lack adequate inline comments, external documentation, or design specifications—original developers have often retired, taking institutional knowledge with them. This creates a fundamental documentation gap: to safely migrate, refactor, or rewrite these systems, engineers need accurate descriptions of what each program does, yet manual documentation at scale is prohibitively expensive given the extensive codebases requiring analysis.Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities in code understanding and documentation generation. Multiple frontier models, including GPT-4, Claude, LLaMA, and specialized code models, can generate human-readable summaries of code functionality. This creates an opportunity to automatically document legacy COBOL codebases at scale. However, a fundamental question remains: How do we evaluate the quality, accuracy, and reliability of AI-generated documentation when no ground truth exists? Traditional code summarization research relies on reference-based metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore) that measure similarity against human-authored reference summaries. These metrics are inapplicable to legacy COBOL scenarios where no reference documentation exists.LLM-based approaches. Existing approaches to assessing LLM output quality offer partial solutions but are insufficient in isolation. Reference-based metrics (BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002)), ROUGE ( (Lin, 2004)), CodeBLEU ( (Ren et al., 2020)), BERTScore ( (Zhang et al., 2019)) require human-authored ground truth summaries—fundamentally inapplicable when no reference documentation exists. Model-internal confidence signals such as perplexity and logit probabilities provide valuable indicators of generation uncertainty and can flag when models are uncertain about their predictions. However, these token-level signals cannot reliably detect when a model is confidently wrong about semantic interpretation—a model may generate a fluent, high-probability summary that completely misinterprets business logic. Single-model LLM-as-judge approaches where one model evaluates another’s output show promise but face validity concerns: evaluators may have systematic biases or blind spots, lack deep understanding of COBOL-specific constructs and mainframe paradigms, have no ground truth for calibration, and can themselves produce inconsistent assessments. No single metric adequately addresses the multifaceted challenge of reference-free evaluation for domain-specific legacy code.Challenge: No human-authored references. In the absence of human-authored references, how can we quantitatively estimate confidence in LLM-generated COBOL documentation to determine which outputs are reliable enough for operational use and which require human expert review? This requires evaluation metrics that are: reference-free (operable without ground truth comparisons); quantifiable (producing numerical confidence scores supporting prioritization and quality gating); interpretable (providing actionable signals explaining why outputs are flagged as low-confidence); multi-dimensional (assessing correctness, completeness, and consistency across multiple quality axes); robust (resistant to single-model biases and prompt engineering artifacts); and scalable (applicable to millions of lines of code requiring documentation). For enterprise adoption, organizations need confidence metrics that indicate: “This summary has high inter-model agreement and complete code coverage—safe for downstream use” versus “This summary has contradictions and potential omissions—requires expert review.”Our approach: overview. We propose a multi-metric ensemble framework that combines complementary evaluation mechanisms:
(1)Inter-model agreement via LLM-as-judge: generating summaries from multiple diverse models and employing structured pairwise comparisons;
(2)Calibrated aggregation: combining judgments through linear pooling with conjunctive penalty for corroborated contradictions;
(3)Token-level confidence scores: measuring generation certainty through perplexity and logit probability analysis;
(4)Code coverage assessment: employing G-Eval metrics to quantify documentation completeness.This reference-free framework enables automatic triage of AI-generated documentation.Our approach has been implemented inside Infosys to deal with summarization of large code bases and extraction of business rules from those code bases for developers. This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 contains backgroun and related work. Section 3 describes our approach in detail. Section 4 describes the evaluation of our approach and results, and Section 5 concludes the paper.
2.Background and Related Work
CODE-NN (Iyer et al., 2016) introduced the first fully data-driven, end-to-end neural approach to code summarization, using LSTM networks with an attention mechanism to generate natural language descriptions of C# code snippets and SQL queries. The model was trained on a corpus automatically mined from StackOverflow, sidestepping the need for hand-labeled data. Building on this attentional encoder-decoder paradigm, code2vec (Alon et al., 2019) took a different angle, representing code as a fixed-length vector by decomposing it into paths through its abstract syntax tree (AST) and learning to aggregate those paths; trained on roughly 14 million methods, it was shown to predict method names accurately even on previously unseen code and to capture meaningful semantic relationships between code snippets. Code2seq (Alon et al., 2018) extended this AST-path idea into a full sequence-generation setting, using attention over the same compositional AST paths to decode natural language sequences rather than single labels, and it outperformed prior token-sequence-based neural machine translation models across multiple languages and tasks, including code summarization and code captioning.DeepCom (Hu et al., 2018) approached the problem as a structure-aware machine translation task, applying NLP techniques together with structural information extracted from Java methods to automatically generate descriptive comments, and it demonstrated clear gains in BLEU-4 scores over earlier baselines like CODE-NN by better capturing the semantics of source code rather than just its token sequence. Finally, the Transformer-based approach of Ahmad et al. (Ahmad et al., 2020) replaced recurrent architectures with a self-attention Transformer model for encoding code, finding that relative position encoding of code tokens (rather than the absolute encoding used in standard Transformers) substantially improved performance; combined with copy attention, this simple adaptation outperformed prior state-of-the-art techniques by a significant margin and has since become a common baseline architecture in the field. Together, these five papers trace the field’s progression from RNN/LSTM-based sequence models, through AST-path-based structural representations, to Transformer architectures explicitly adapted to the syntactic properties of code.Code summarization models are commonly evaluated using a combination of lexical overlap, syntactic awareness, and semantic similarity metrics. BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) measures the n-gram overlap between a generated summary and one or more reference summaries, emphasizing precision by rewarding exact word sequence matches. ROUGE (Lin, 2004) focuses on recall and evaluates how much of the reference summary is captured by the generated text, with variants such as ROUGE-N and ROUGE-L measuring n-gram and longest common subsequence overlap, respectively. To better assess code-related text generation, CodeBLEU (Ren et al., 2020) extends BLEU by incorporating programming-language-specific features, including weighted n-gram matching, abstract syntax tree (AST) similarity, and data-flow consistency, providing a more comprehensive evaluation of code understanding and generation quality. In contrast, BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2019) leverages contextual embeddings from pre-trained transformer models to measure semantic similarity between generated and reference summaries, allowing it to capture meaning even when different words or phrasing are used. Together, these metrics provide complementary perspectives on code summarization quality, ranging from surface-level lexical agreement to deeper semantic and structural correctness.
3.Approach
A high level view of our approach is depicted in Figure 1. The first step of the approach includes parsing and static analysis of the COBOL code to understand dependencies among paragraphs, build a call graph, and extract other types of information. The output of this step is a set of code chunks, each of which is summarized as a unit in the next steps. Determining the correct granularity of this step is an important aspect of our approach. At one end, chunks at the level of single instructions create verbose descriptions that are not useful. At another extreme, chunks that include whole programs create summaries that hide important details and are not useful. After experimenting with different granularities, we settle for chunks at the paragraph and function level.Let C denote a COBOL code chunk dedicated to a single functionality. Importantly, the chunking policy is not under our control: the segmentation into summarisation units is predetermined by the Infosys pipeline. Our method therefore treats the Infosys chunking as fixed and operates downstream. This constraint reflects realistic deployment conditions, where third-party enterprise tooling governs preprocessing.We assume a set of auxiliary descriptions for called paragraphs or programs, 𝒟={(ni,di)}i=1m, where ni is a callee name and di is a fixed, vetted English description. These include descriptions of called paragraphs/functions. These dependency descriptions are injected into prompts and not reconstructed per run, both to reduce variance and to keep the evaluation focused on the behaviour of C. In addition, the prompt is also augmented with a list of criteria L={L1,…,Ln} specifying the task to the LLM and the outputs (See Appendix for the list used in the evaluation). Specifically, the list L contains the criteria decided by Infosys in their prompt.We consider three summarisation systems:M0=Infosys (OpenAI-based),M1=LLaMA 3.3-70B,M2=Grok-3.Given a prompt template aligned with Infosys’ style (to control granularity), each model produces a summary:S0←M0​(C,𝒟),S1←M1​(C,𝒟),S2←M2​(C,𝒟).Model diversity is desirable but the method is agnostic to the specific choices so long as the models are competent summarizers and not identically trained; the ensemble logic extends to k>3 models.Figure 1.Overview of the ensemble-based confidence estimation pipeline. A COBOL code chunk and its dependencies are summarised by three models (Infosys, LLaMA 3.3–70B, Grok–3). Pairwise comparisons with an LLM-as-judge yield structured scores, which are then aggregated into a final confidence estimate.

3.1.Pairwise Evaluation via LLM-as-Judge
Traditional reference-based metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore) correlate imperfectly with human judgments for code summarisation and are sensitive to surface form and identifier overlap—a poor fit for reference-free settings. Prompted LLM judges, by contrast, have shown strong correlation with human ratings on code tasks (Wu et al., 2024; Robinson and Kummerfeld, 2025). We therefore instantiate a dedicated OpenAI model 𝒥 as an evaluator that compares pairs of summaries following a list of criteria L={L1,…,Ln} specifying the task to the LLM and the outputs (See Appendix for the list used in the evaluation).
Anchored, pairwise comparisons.
We conduct two comparisons anchored on the Infosys output:E1=𝒥⁡(S1,S0),E2=𝒥⁡(S2,S0).Each evaluation returns a structured JSON record
Ei=(agreementi,scorei,missing_detailsi,contradictionsi,rationalei).The agreement label is one of Agree/Mostly Agree/Disagree; the score is a continuous confidence on [0,10] tied to a list of criteria that emphasises functional equivalence (purpose, logic, inputs, outputs) and discounts mere wording differences. The missing-details and contradictions fields enumerate omissions and logical conflicts, respectively, and the rationale gives a concise justification. These fields serve both downstream explainability and manual auditability.
Granularity control.
A common failure mode in pairwise judging is spurious disagreement caused by mismatched levels of detail. To mitigate this, all generators use prompts that mirror Infosys’ template, and evaluators are instructed to: (i) ignore stylistic paraphrase; (ii) treat minor omissions as Mostly Agree if they do not alter semantics; and (iii) reserve Disagree for contradictions or omissions that change behaviour. This alignment makes disagreements diagnostic rather than an artefact of verbosity mismatches.
3.2.Aggregation: Linear Pooling with Conjunctive Penalty
Let ai∈{Agree,Mostly Agree,Disagree} and si∈[0,10] denote the label and confidence produced by Ei. Define the support contributed by each judge asui={si,ai∈{Agree,Mostly Agree},0,ai=Disagree,and the base support as the linear opinion poolu¯=12​(u1+u2).This is the equal-weight linear pool, preserving interpretability (two 10s average to 10) and reflecting the standard practice of combining expert scores via averaging.We then apply a conjunctive penalty to encode corroborated negative evidence. Let 𝟏​[⋅] be the indicator and define the disagreement strength for a judge asdi={5−si5∈[0,1],ai=Disagree,0,otherwise.Intuitively, a Disagree accompanied by si≈5 is weak (di≈0), whereas si≈0 is strong (di≈1). Let Pmax∈[0,5] be a hyperparameter. The final score isConf=clamp(u¯− 1[a1=Disagree∧a2=Disagree]⋅Pmax⋅d1+d22, 0, 10)That is, we subtract a penalty only if both judges disagree, and we scale that penalty by the average strength of their disagreement. When only one judge disagrees, its support is already zero; we do not double-penalise, which improves robustness to single-rater noise.The rule combines two standard ideas: equal-weight linear opinion pooling for supportive evidence and a k-of-n (conjunctive) decision fusion for negative evidence. If a false Disagree occurs with probability α per judge, the chance that both are false is α2, so penalising only the 2-of-2 case reduces the expected false penalty from α to α2 under approximate independence. Empirically, this yields cleaner separation for triage: cases with two emphatic Disagrees are pushed decisively low, while “contested” cases (e.g., 10 vs. 5-Disagree) remain in the middle for human review.
Illustrative outcomes.
With Pmax=3.5:
•(10,Agree) and (5,Disagree) ⇒u¯=5.0, no penalty ⇒Conf=5.0.
•(3,Disagree) and (2,Disagree) ⇒u¯=0.0; mean d=0.5; penalty 1.75 ⇒Conf=0.0 after clamp.
•(5,Disagree) and (5,Disagree) ⇒u¯=0.0; mean d=0; penalty 0 ⇒Conf=0.0.
3.3.Token-Level Confidence via Perplexity
While inter-model agreement provides evidence of semantic consistency, it does not capture the generation certainty of individual summaries. A model may produce a fluent output that agrees with others yet internally exhibit high uncertainty during generation. To address this, we incorporate token-level confidence scores derived from the model’s output probability distribution.
Logit probabilities and perplexity.
Modern LLM APIs support returning log-probabilities for generated tokens when the logprobs parameter is enabled. For each token ti in a generated summary S={t1,t2,…,tn}, the model provides log⁡P⁡(ti∣t<i,C), representing the log-probability of token ti given the preceding context and COBOL input C. We compute the perplexity of a generated summary as(1)PPL(S)=exp(−1n∑i=1nlogP(ti∣t<i,C)).Perplexity measures how “surprised” the model is by its own generation: lower perplexity indicates higher confidence, while higher perplexity suggests the model struggled to predict subsequent tokens. For enterprise applications, perplexity provides a reference-free signal identifying generations where the model exhibited uncertainty—even if the output appears superficially fluent.
Confidence score normalization.
Raw perplexity values are model-specific and domain-dependent. We normalize scores to [0,10] using(2)Confppl​(S)=10×clamp⁡(1−PPL⁡(S)−PPLminPPLmax−PPLmin, 0, 1),where PPLmin and PPLmax are calibrated thresholds from a held-out validation set of COBOL summaries (Figure 2). This yields an interpretable score where 10 indicates maximum certainty and 0 indicates the model was highly uncertain during generation.
Threshold calibration.
Because perplexity is unbounded on [1,∞) and its absolute scale varies across models and domains, raw values are neither directly interpretable nor comparable with the other [0,10] metrics. The thresholds PPLmin and PPLmax anchor the mapping of Equation (2): PPLmin marks the “confident” end (mapped to confidence 10) and PPLmax the “uncertain” end (mapped to confidence 0), with linear interpolation in between and clamping outside. Both are estimated from the perplexity distribution over a held-out set of COBOL summaries, keeping the metric reference-free yet calibrated to the deployment model and corpus.PPLmin=1.2PPLmax=8.50246810Perplexity PPL⁡(S)Confppl​(S)Figure 2.Perplexity-to-confidence normalization (Equation (2)). Summaries with PPL≤PPLmin saturate at maximum score 10; score decreases linearly to 0 at PPLmax and is clamped beyond. The plot shows: constant score of 10 for PPL≤1.2; linear decrease from 10 to 0 over interval [1.2,8.5]; constant score of 0 for PPL≥8.5.

Integration with ensemble scores.
Perplexity complements the inter-model agreement framework:
•A summary with high inter-model agreement and low perplexity (high Confppl) is strongly validated.
•A summary with high inter-model agreement but high perplexity may indicate convergence on a challenging interpretation that warrants additional review.
•A summary with low inter-model agreement and high perplexity clearly signals unreliability.We combine these signals through weighted averaging:(3)Confbase=α⋅Conf+(1−α)⋅Confppl,α∈[0.6,0.8],where Conf is the aggregated confidence and α weights ensemble agreement more heavily (as it captures semantic correctness), while perplexity provides a complementary generation-quality signal.
3.4.Code Coverage Assessment via G-Eval
A critical failure mode unaddressed by pairwise comparison and perplexity is omission: a model may generate a confident, internally consistent summary that simply fails to document significant portions of the input code. Reference-based metrics like BLEU cannot detect omissions without ground-truth coverage annotations. We therefore introduce a coverage-aware metric adapted from G-Eval (Liu et al., 2023)—a framework that uses LLMs as evaluators with chain-of-thought reasoning.
G-Eval for summarization coverage.
Given a COBOL code chunk C and a generated summary S, we prompt an LLM evaluator ℰ to assess coverage:
“You are an expert code reviewer. Given the following COBOL code and its summary, evaluate the code coverage of the summary. Code coverage measures whether the summary accounts for all significant logic: procedure divisions, conditional branches, file I/O operations, data transformations, and control flow. Identify any code segments omitted by the summary. Rate coverage on a scale of 1–5: 5: All significant code paths documented; 4: Minor omissions (e.g., edge cases); 3: Moderate omissions; 2: Significant portions undocumented; 1: Summary misses critical logic. Provide a brief rationale explaining your rating.”The evaluator returns a structured response consisting of a coverage score, identified missing segments, and justification rationale.
Aggregated coverage score.
To ensure robustness, we query the evaluator k times (temperature >0 for diversity) and aggregate:(4)Cov⁡(S,C)=2k​∑i=1kcoverage​_​scorei∈[2,10].We use k=3 for cost-efficiency while achieving stable estimates (empirically, variance stabilizes beyond k=3). Because each run returns an integer rubric score in {1,…,5}, with k=3 the aggregate takes values in {2.0,2.67,…,9.33,10.0}; the factor of 2 rescales the 1–5 scale to [2,10] for consistency with the other confidence metrics, where higher values indicate better coverage.COBOL chunk C   +   summary SG-Eval coverage prompt(1–5 rubric + criteria)Eval run 2Eval run 1Eval run kCov⁡(S,C)=2k​∑i=1kcovi∈[2,10]Conffinal=Confbase×Cov⁡(S,C)10Figure 3.Coverage assessment via G-Eval. The (chunk, summary) pair is scored k times (τ>0) on a 1–5 rubric; scores are averaged and rescaled to [2,10] (Equation (4)), then applied as multiplicative penalty to base confidence (Equation (5)).

Detection of systematic omissions.
Beyond numerical scores, G-Eval’s rationale field enables qualitative analysis. If multiple evaluations identify the same missing segments (e.g., “file error handling not mentioned”), this provides actionable feedback for human reviewers or model fine-tuning.
Why G-Eval over heuristics?
Naive coverage metrics might count lines of code mentioned or perform keyword matching (e.g., checking if all COBOL verbs appear in the summary). However, such heuristics fail to capture semantic coverage: a summary might mention “file operations” without explaining what those operations do. "Scores 48.5% on the test." Almost every AI launch leads with a benchmark number. Here's what that actually means, in 60 seconds.

→ A benchmark is a standard test: the same questions or tasks given to every model, so scores can be compared
→ Like an exam, it measures one skill. A coding test tells you little about writing or maths
→ Most launch numbers are the company's own results, not independent tests

Why to be careful:
→ Tests go out of date fast. Stanford's AI Index found scores on the SWE-bench coding test rose 67 points in a single year
→ A model can be tuned to pass a test without getting better at real work. Researchers call this overfitting
→ Companies choose which tests to put in the launch post

How to read one: who ran it, which version of the model, compared with what, and does it match the job you need done?

The takeaway: a benchmark is a clue, not a verdict. Test it on your own task.

An LLM judge flagged about 18% of AI agents' output tokens as removable waste. The task and the harness explain more of that waste than the model does.

Huimin Zeng (@siebelschool), @leoleoasd_cn and @dakuowang (@Northeastern), @DiWu0162, @Eric1706291394, @gordonhu608 and @kaiwei_chang (@ucla), @jiaxin_pei (@UTAustin) and coauthors built a meter for token waste.

The harness base URL points at a @LiteLLM proxy that logs every call. The judge marks removable spans as restate, duplicate fetch, padding or detour. The framework deletes those spans and recounts tokens with each provider's tokenizer.

They tested the label by acting on it. Online pruning of restate and padding removed 41% of Kimi-K3 reasoning on SWE-bench Verified, and 89.5% of tasks were still solved (89.0% before). On MCP-Atlas, pruning 46% of reasoning gave 62.3% solved (65.0% before). Deleting all reasoning cut success to 73.0% and 56.0%.

Across 6 frontier models, waste varied more by benchmark than by model. Detours were the largest share for most models.

With the same model and effort, reasoning volume changed more than 4x across harnesses. Three harnesses opened the SWE-bench Verified shell in the wrong Python environment. Kimi Code CLI's shell schema allowed timeouts up to 86,400 s, but its runtime rejected anything above 300 s.

Raising Kimi-K3 from High to Max effort cost 0.80M more tokens with no measurable gain.

My takeaway: audit the harness before you swap the model.

Evaluating AI agents involves moving beyond simple metrics toward rigorous, multi-dimensional assessment. In his talk, Alex Ratner outlines that because AI capabilities now outpace traditional measurement, we must adopt more sophisticated, realistic testing environments .

Ratner identifies three key axes to effectively benchmark modern AI agents:

Environment Complexity: Moving from isolated, self-contained tasks (like basic coding exams) to messy, real-world contexts. This requires agents to navigate tools, interfaces (like OSWorld 2.0), and messy repositories 

Autonomy Horizon: Measuring an agent’s performance on long-term, dynamic tasks. This assesses not just the ability to complete a single step, but to adapt when goals shift, demonstrating capabilities like continual learning.

Nuanced Verifiability: Shifting away from binary unit tests (which only check if an answer is "correct") toward evaluating qualitative output. This includes judging code quality, architectural decision-making, and stylistic "taste," such as in Senior SWE-bench.

To prevent "benchmaxxing" (overfitting to public leaderboards), Ratner emphasizes that organizations should prioritize continuous benchmarks that evolve like open-source projects, ensuring they remain robust and resistant to being gamed.

🌊 Ripple-65B Preview puts a dense 65B model into the agentic coding race, with downloadable weights and a surprisingly low API price.

Ricursive Intelligence built it as a general-purpose variant of the model behind its AI chip design platform. The release includes BF16 and NVFP4 instruction-tuned checkpoints, plus a BF16 base model, under Apache 2.0.

🧩 The architecture takes a fairly deliberate route: 80 layers, a 5,120-wide hidden state, sliding-window and global attention, gated attention, activation clipping, and value residuals. Pretraining used 12 trillion tokens of text and code; the instruction model advertises up to 1,048,576 tokens of context.

The team also built its own synthetic post-training data pipelines rather than buying post-training datasets. Its RL recipe combines truncated importance sampling, score centering, and a linear length penalty.

📊 Ricursive's reported results against Reflection Beam:

▪️ Terminal-Bench 2.1: 80.5 vs. 80.1.
▪️ SWE-bench Pro v2.0 Hard: 79.1 vs. 76.5.
▪️ SWE-bench Verified: 76.5 vs. 81.6.
▪️ GPQA Diamond: 85.2 vs. 90.6.

That is a strong coding profile, with clear trade-offs across tasks. These are developer-reported comparisons mixing official scores with in-house evaluations. Ricursive explicitly warns that harness choices and context handling shift agentic benchmark results.

The parameter comparison needs care, too: Beam has 501B total parameters but 23B active per token, while dense Ripple activates all 65B. Total model size alone does not tell you the inference cost.

💸 Ricursive puts the full development bill at $32 million, including architecture experiments, data work, debugging, synthetic generation, and final training. Its claim that this is one-tenth of the previous leader's cost is the company's estimate.

Together AI lists $0.20 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens. Check the endpoint's actual context limit: its page currently mixes 128K and 1M descriptions. Fireworks currently lists dedicated deployment with no serverless support, so the same per-token offer should not be assumed there.

📦 NVFP4 weights make local experimentation more accessible, but a million-token context still carries substantial memory overhead. The useful test is how reliably Ripple finishes your repository tasks at an acceptable total cost.

In Feburary, OpenAI stopped publishing results on SWE-bench Verified (where for some tasks, models from 3 labs, including GPT-5.2, can replicate the reference fix from the task ID or short hint). HumanEval is even worse. It consists of 164 tasks at an easy interview question level (as stated by the authors). It has been heavily boasted about in announcements of coding models over the past few years. NVIDIA ran testing using 10 models and found a correlation of around -0.4. That means there is an inverse correlation. The higher the HumanEval score, the worse the agent performed on average after fine-tuning in this sample.

The new benchmark is from NVIDIA (Paper: Before They Can Solve by 22 authors). They use a log of a strong agent solving a real task and identify the critical step. This is the first edit that makes the projects tests pass. They run testing on the base model. One of the 3 checks is how obvious this step is to the model. When ranked by this metric, the order of the 10 models matched the final rankings with a correlation of ~0.96.

The approach is a nice one, and I like it. However, it relies heavily on the SWE-bench Verified test which was abandoned by OpenAI. While they have validated using other benchmarks, there are only 10 models and no confidence intervals. They state the numbers are descriptive. They require logs of an agent stronger than the one you're selecting. This means it isn't very useful for the top ones. There are no values for cost (which is the whole point). One of the logs for their own model Nemotron-3-Ultra had an inflated score.

The market for agents is similar. Only around 130 out of thousands of vendors stating that they have an agentic product actually do (Gartner estimate). Over 40% of agent projects will be abandoned by the end of 2027 (Gartner forecast). Anthropic have some interesting guidance. Claude Opus 4.5 scored 42% on CORE-Bench. However, they found issues in the test itself. The check marked their answer down as it was expecting 96.124991 but they had answered with 96.12. After fixing the issues and changing the harness, it scored 95%.

If I were a company looking to select an agent, I would only look at the leaderboards for initial filtering. I would gather 20-50 private tasks (Anthropic recommend you start with this amount) from my own tracker. These should have an accepted solution and tests. Silicon Valley venture capitalists are pouring billions into foundation models, humanoid assembly lines, and physical AI compute clusters.

They all obsess over the same talking points: H100 vs B200 chip allocations, memory bandwidth, model parameter scale, and synthetic training data.

Almost none of them are paying attention to the real bottleneck waiting at the substation gate: high-voltage utility transformers.

If you want to build a gigafactory for bipedal robots or spin up a 100,000-GPU cluster, you do not just plug into the local power grid. You need high-capacity step-down transformers to drop 345kV transmission voltage down to usable industrial levels.

Lead times for large power transformers in the United States currently sit between 3 and 4 years.

Why the delay?

First, grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES). High-efficiency transformer cores require specialized magnetic steel with specific crystal orientations to minimize eddy current losses. Only a handful of mills on Earth can manufacture it at scale, and global supply is severely backlogged.

Second, skilled manual labor. Winding high-voltage copper and aluminum coils for 100MVA transformers is not fully automated. It requires experienced coil winders, and the workforce has been shrinking for two decades.

Third, regulatory queue bottlenecks. Interconnection queues with regional transmission operators like PJM and ERCOT now stretch past 2029 for major industrial loads.

This is why companies like Tesla and hyperscalers are quietly stockpiling utility transformers on open gravel lots and buying up gas turbine rental fleets.

They know compute hardware is easy to buy. Getting 100 megawatts of physical power delivered to your building is the actual competitive moat.

Without transformers, your supercomputer is just a very expensive warehouse of silicon bricks.

Sparse attention has a search problem: attending to a small set of tokens can be cheap, while finding that set still means scanning the context.

Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), from Prefrontal AI and ETH Zurich, targets that bottleneck. The paper's 22.7× result is worth unpacking because it connects three things that often get blurred together: the retrieval algorithm, the GPU implementation, and end-to-end serving.

Start with the bottleneck.

In the authors' GLM-5.3-Flash experiment at 10M tokens, indexing takes 98% of a sparse attention layer's prefill time. That measurement is for one global attention layer on one H200, processing the final 32,768-query chunk. It is not a breakdown of the entire model's runtime.

A fixed attention budget does not fix this by itself. If every query still scores every earlier key or block to find its candidates, the indexer remains quadratic over a full prefill.

LSA changes how those candidates are organized and searched.

For the distilled variant, D-LSA, the base model stays frozen. Small query/key projections learn a 64-dimensional indexing space by matching the model's attention distribution. The authors distill these indexers on 352M tokens; they do not then fine-tune the whole model under the new sparse attention.

At inference, the process is roughly:

1. Normalize the index keys and pool consecutive keys in groups of four.
2. Within completed 512-token blocks, cluster the pooled keys by similarity into buckets. Cache each bucket's centroid and the positions of its keys.
3. Score bucket centroids with the query, then expand selected buckets into a bounded list of long-range key indices.
4. Run the model's attention on those original keys and values, plus sink tokens and a recent-token window.

The buckets can group non-adjacent tokens within a block, rather than being defined only by contiguous position. The KV cache is retained. At the 10M-token setting, D-LSA selects up to 4,096 long-range keys per query, alongside 4 sink keys and a 512-token window.

There are two search paths, and their claims need to stay separate.

D-LSA (Flat) scans all bucket centroids. It reduces the work substantially, but its prefill indexer is still asymptotically quadratic.

D-LSA (Tree) builds a hierarchy over the buckets and uses beam search. With a fixed beam width, the indexer scores O(log T) centroids per query, giving O(T log T) prefill indexing. This is the subquadratic path.

The headline 22.7× speedup comes from Flat, not evidence that Tree is already the best choice at every measured length. The paper's performance predictions beyond 10M tokens are extrapolations. In the main benchmark, its single-request Tree decode results also use Flat search, rather than demonstrating tree-search decode speedups.

The implementation matters too. For long-context Flat prefill, the scoring kernel filters candidates while the scores are still on chip, instead of writing the entire query-by-centroid score matrix to GPU memory. The indexer includes clustering, scoring, selection and expansion kernels. Sparse attention still needs an efficient search implementation to turn fewer candidates into lower latency.

Now the performance numbers, with their boundaries attached.

For GLM-5.3-Flash at 10M tokens on one H200, the authors report D-LSA (Flat) at:

• 22.7× faster prefill
• 4.6× faster decode

The baseline is GLM's existing block-sparse attention. These are timings of the whole attention module, including projections, indexing and attention. Prefill measures the final 32,768-query chunk; decode measures one step of one request, with clustering amortized across steps.

For the whole GLM model in SGLang on 8× H200 with context/expert parallelism, the corresponding 10M-token results are:

• 2.24× speedup in time to first token
• 2.10× speedup in time per output token

Those serving measurements use one request at a time and the median of three requests generating 256 tokens. Only the global attention layers get faster; the rest of the model still has its cost. The single-layer gain is therefore much larger than the end-to-end gain.

Qwen-3.8-27B has a different baseline: full attention. At 10M tokens, the authors report 72.4×/42.5× single-layer prefill/decode speedups on H200, and 9.21×/2.87× end-to-end TTFT/TPOT speedups on eight H200s. Those numbers answer a different comparison from replacing GLM's already-sparse attention.

Accuracy is the other half of the result.

For Qwen, D-LSA (Flat) scores 63.9 versus 59.9 for full attention on RULER at 10M tokens. For GLM, Flat trails its sparse baseline by up to 8 points at 2M–5M tokens and is within 4 points at 10M.

Tree introduces another trade-off: on GLM at 10M tokens, RULER falls to 55.8 with Tree versus 66.8 with Flat. Better asymptotic search cost does not guarantee the same retrieval quality.

These are benchmark results beyond the models' advertised context windows, using subsets where evaluation is expensive. RULER uses 20 prompts per task above 1M tokens. They support a promising speed/accuracy trade-off, not a blanket claim of lossless attention or reliable performance on every 10M-token workload.

The paper also explores N-LSA, trained from scratch using only next-token loss. It clusters the attention's own keys and needs no separate index projections or distillation teacher.

That evidence comes from a roughly 0.5B-parameter hybrid model, Flat search, and contexts up to 128k. At 128k, the authors report matching validation loss, a 1.6× single-layer training speedup, and a 1.24× faster whole-model decay phase. Peak per-layer training memory is higher: 6.8 GiB versus 5.8 GiB. Larger native models, longer contexts and native Tree training remain open.

All numbers here are the authors' reported results; I have not reproduced them.

For AI engineers, the useful conclusion is that sparse attention's retrieval cost deserves its own design and measurement. LSA shows that learned semantic grouping can make that search much cheaper. Flat delivers the strongest headline measured speedup, while Tree offers a better scaling path with accuracy and crossover costs. The full KV cache still grows linearly with context, so efficient selection advances ultra-long-context inference without solving its storage cost.

GPU Compute Spot and Derivatives

The Flop Network design treats GPU compute as a measurable commodity with a spot layer and a derivatives layer. The delivery layer needs a standard unit covering accelerator model, memory, location, uptime, latency, software image, and the time interval supplied. A contract referencing an H100-hour can settle incorrectly when two providers deliver materially different configurations under the same label. The measurement layer therefore needs signed telemetry, independent verification, and a dispute window. The pricing layer must define whether the reference is a cleared trade, a provider quote, an auction result, or a volume-weighted index. Sparse trading can leave the index stale while derivatives continue to reprice. The collateral layer sets initial margin, maintenance margin, liquidation thresholds, and the waterfall used when compute prices move faster than positions can close. The custody layer may hold stablecoins or other assets whose own volatility can weaken the margin buffer. Physical delivery creates additional boundaries: a buyer needs credentials, networking, data transfer, and access to the promised cluster at the scheduled time. Cash settlement removes delivery logistics but introduces basis risk between the index and the actual cost of obtaining compute. Privileged keys can alter provider admission, index inputs, or emergency settlement. Oracle manipulation, sequencer interruption, false telemetry, double allocation of one cluster, and supplier insolvency are direct failure modes. Contract rules also need to cover hardware substitution, regional export controls, maintenance downtime, force majeure, and early termination. The control stack is complete only when a participant can trace the reference price, verify delivered capacity, challenge an incorrect measurement, and reach a defined collateral endpoint after default.

Two caveats before anyone gets excited. All performance numbers are the publisher's own, and I couldn't verify the licence or the terms on the weights. I'd want an independent run before quoting those timings.

That said — the direction is clear. 
The gap between "needs a cluster" and "needs the GPU you already own" keeps collapsing, and audio is coming along for the ride now.

CMU Deep Learning Systems — Lecture 19: Training Large Models

Activation checkpointing saves selected boundaries and reconstructs the missing activations when backward needs them.

In a uniform N-layer chain, checkpointing every K layers gives a storage proxy N/K + K. Balancing the two terms suggests K near √N. For a constructed 64-layer case, the proxy reaches 16 activation units at K = 8; this is not a measurement of total GPU memory.

The same lecture connects memory lifetimes with distributed execution: data parallelism must preserve the loss denominator, and communication can overlap backward work only when its inputs are ready. More GPUs do not remove those dependencies.

Qwen3.8-27B refused to answer a question about the Tiananmen Square events of June 1989.

Arete-27B, a Nous Research supervised fine-tune of Qwen3.8-27B, gave a direct historical response, describing the military crackdown on pro-democracy protests and the killing of protesters.

Both models were asked the same question:

“What happened at Tiananmen Square in June 1989?”

This is an interesting comparison because Arete-27B shares Qwen3.8-27B’s underlying architecture, but its post-training produces different response behaviour.

Running Arete-27B locally

The developer also demonstrated Arete-27B running on a single NVIDIA RTX 3060 with just 12GB VRAM.

Reported performance:

• Context window: 158K tokens
• Decode speed: ~22 tokens/s
• Prefill speed: ~490 tokens/s
• GPU: RTX 3060 12GB
• Quantisation: IQ2_XS

The model uses aggressive weight quantisation and a Q4_0 KV cache to fit the workload within the available memory.

Configuration

The setup uses llama.cpp’s llama-server:

llama-server \
  -m NousResearch_Arete-27B-IQ2_XS.gguf \
  -ngl 99 \
  -c 158000 \
  -fa on \
  --jinja \
  -np 1 \
  --cache-type-k q4_0 \
  --cache-type-v q4_0 \
  --temp 1.0 \
  --top-p 0.95 \
  --top-k 20 \
  --min-p 0.0 \
  --presence-penalty 0.0 \
  --repeat-penalty 1.0 \
  --reasoning on

A few settings stand out:

• IQ2_XS: Compresses the model weights aggressively to reduce memory requirements.

• 158K context: Configures the server to accept a large context, although actual speed can vary with context length.

• Flash Attention: Enabled to improve attention computation efficiency.

• Q4_0 KV cache: Reduces the memory used to store keys and values during inference.

• Single parallel sequence: Keeps the setup focused on one active request.

What the comparison shows

The experiment highlights two separate aspects of local model development.

First, a 27B model can run on a 12GB consumer GPU with sufficiently aggressive quantisation and careful memory management.

Second, sharing the same architecture doesn’t mean two models will respond identically. Fine-tuning and post-training choices can influence refusal behaviour and how models handle politically sensitive questions.

The Tiananmen example is one test, not proof that Arete will answer every sensitive question or that it is generally more capable than Qwen3.8-27B.

Still, it’s a useful demonstration of how much model behaviour can change without changing the underlying architecture. https://t.co/b6Z6fOH0Qm

财联社11月9日讯（记者夏淑媛） 新一期财联社“C50风向指数”结果显示，10月金融数据或将呈现社融改善、信贷收缩的态势。信贷方面，10月新增人民币贷款或再现负值，市场机构预测中值为-1500亿元；同期新增社融预测中值为1.5万亿元，或实现同比多增6800亿元。货币增速来看，10月末M1、M2同比增速或双双小幅回落。

物价方面，国家统计局今日公布数据显示，10月CPI同比上涨0.7%，PPI同比上涨5.7%刷新年内新高。而此前市场机构对10月CPI同比增速的预测中值为0.8%，对PPI的预测中值为5.3%，实际数据与预测值整体契合。

“C50风向指数调查”是由财联社发起，由市场中的各类研究机构参与完成，结果能够较为全面地反映市场机构对于宏观经济走势、货币政策感受以及金融数据的预期。共有近20家机构参与本期调查。

10月新增人民币贷款或同比少增，市场预测中值为-1500亿元

9月新增人民币贷款录得1.08万亿元，虽同比少增2100亿元，但较8月的600亿元大幅回升，略超市场预期。

本期调查显示，10月新增人民币贷款或再现负值，难改同比少增格局。市场机构预测中值为-1500亿元，较去年同期的2200亿元少增3700亿元，预测区间在-2000亿元至3000亿元。

市场人士指出，10月是季末集中冲量后的传统信贷“小月”，银行投放节奏通常随之放缓，主要受以下两方面因素影响：

一方面，居民端融资需求整体偏弱，新增贷款或出现负值。

从消费端看，财通证券研究所固收首席隋修平表示，10月下旬地铁出行强于季节性，但乘用车零售、电影票房偏弱，消费修复仍有分化，预计居民短贷环比多减、同比少减。

从房贷端看，高频数据显示，10月1日-29日，30大中城市商品房成交面积约543.7万平方米，较去年同期下降16.1%。隋修平认为，虽有一线城市住房成交形成一定支撑，但重点城市新房成交总体仍不及去年同期，局部改善对按揭需求全面修复的带动效果尚需观测，预计居民中长期贷款环比转负、同比多减。

另一方面，企业端融资缺乏扩张基础，信贷同比或多减。

隋修平指出，受10月制造业指数降至49.8%及季初回落影响，企业经营周转需求偏弱，预计企业短贷环比转负、同比少减；同时，建筑业指数降至48.0%且基建实物工作量传导不畅，预计中长贷同比少增。整体来看，短贷的同比少减难以抵消中长贷的回落，企业融资仍缺乏持续扩张的基础。

东方金诚宏观首席王青在接受财联社记者采访时表示：“10月新型政策性金融工具投放完毕，预计对企业中长期贷款有一定拉动作用，但难以抵消新增居民贷款为负的影响。”他进一步指出，当前票据利率处于低位且月末未见上冲，既反映信贷需求不强，也预示10月票据冲量现象仍会比较明显。

浙商证券经济学家李超表示：“10月半年期国股银票转贴现利率持续维持在0.5%左右的低位，与10月30日半年期国有大行同业存单利率的利差维持在-90BP左右，这反映出银行票据配置需求较强，而一般贷款需求依然偏弱。”

10月新增社融预测中值1.5万亿元，政策发力有望带动增速回升至7.3%

9月，新增社融规模录得3.55万亿元，同比多增200亿元，较8月同比少增9000亿元的表现明显好转。

本期调查显示，超七成机构预计政策发力有望带动社融存量增速回升至7.3%。市场机构对10月新增社融规模的预测中值为1.5万亿元，较去年同期多增6800亿元，预测区间在1万亿元至1.6万亿元。

王青表示，在投向实体经济的贷款同比多减的背景下，10月新增社融主要由政府债券融资支撑。

具体来看，四季度政府债券融资规模预计较上年同期高出1.5万亿元；单看10月，政府债券融资达1.1万亿元，同比多增约6000亿元；企业债券融资约2900亿元，同比多增近400亿元。

此外，随着10月新型政策性金融工具投放完毕，预计10月单月投放规模或在7000亿元左右，可能带动社融委托贷款同比多增。

货币增速方面，10月末M1及M2同比增速或均小幅回落。

针对M1走势，浙商证券宏观首席林成炜表示：“10月虽然8000亿元新型政策性金融工具已经完成全部投放，但资金补充项目资本金后，还需要经过项目资金拨付及实际支付才能转化为企业交易性存款，对当月M1的直接拉动有限。”其预计10月M1同比增长3.0%，M1与M2剪刀差维持在-4个百分点左右，实体经济资金活化程度仍有待改善。

M2来看，王青分析指出：“一方面，当月新增人民币贷款偏弱，会拖累存款派生；另一方面，四季度稳增长政策发力，有可能带动财政支出提速，若财政存款出现同比少增，则会对M2增速有一定推升作用。”

值得注意的是，近期贸易顺差规模高位上行，叠加人民币持续升值，企业净结汇顺差显著扩大。“这意味着10月还会有较大规模的不计入M2的企业外币资产，转化为纳入M2统计的企业存款，也会阶段性对M2增速形成支撑。”王青表示。

10月CPI同比小幅回落至0.7%，PPI同比升至5.7%刷新年内新高

10月CPI同比上涨0.7%，环比涨幅回落0.2个百分点。此前市场机构预测中值为0.8%，预测区间为0.7%-1.0%。

“10月CPI同比涨幅收窄，主要原因是蔬菜价格大幅下跌，带动食品价格同比降幅显著扩大，充分抵消了当月国际油价上涨推动国内汽油价格上调带来的影响。”王青表示。

兴业银行首席经济学家鲁政委分析指出，受长假需求退坡影响，10月食品价格多数回落。其中猪肉、鸡蛋、蔬菜价格环比分别下跌3.6%、12.6%和8.5%，对食品CPI形成明显拖累。

能源方面，10月国内成品油调价呈现“一搁浅一上调”，交通工具用能源对CPI拉动有限；同时，上海金交所黄金价格环比跌幅扩大至5.7%，拖累其他用品和服务价格。综合食品、能源及黄金价格的表现，叠加翘尾因素，10月CPI同比有所回落。

PPI方面，10月PPI同比上涨5.7%，创2022年7月以来新高，且略超市场预期。 此前，市场普遍预计10月PPI同比将再度刷新年内高点，机构预测中值为5.3%，预测区间为5.1%至5.6%。实际值已突破预测区间上限。

王青表示，10月PPI环比涨幅回落，主要源于当月国际原油、有色金属以及国内煤炭等大宗商品价格在前期较快上涨、绝对价格水平已偏高的背景下，环比上行幅度明显放缓。

“不过，在环比延续上涨带动下，10月PPI同比涨幅进一步扩大。往后看，11月PPI环比可能转跌，同比涨幅将有所回落，但年底前仍将处于4.0%以上的较快增长区间。”王青预计。
